Hydrocarbons.intro: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons that is separated by fractional distillation.

sections.title: Crude Oil
points: Formed from ancient marine organisms over millions of years — non-renewable fossil fuel
Mixture of many different hydrocarbons
Separated by fractional distillation based on boiling point

sections.title: Fractional Distillation
points: Crude oil heated and vaporised; vapours rise up a fractionating column
Column is cooler at the top — temperature gradient
Fractions condense at different levels depending on boiling point
Smaller molecules: lower boiling point, more flammable, less viscous, more volatile
Larger molecules: higher boiling point, more viscous, less flammable
Fractions (top to bottom): gases, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, bitumen

keyTerms.def: A compound containing only carbon and hydrogen
A mixture of hydrocarbons formed from ancient organisms — a fossil fuel
Separation of a mixture based on different boiling points
A group of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points collected at one level

examTips: Shorter carbon chains = lower boiling point = more flammable = less viscous.
Fractional distillation is a PHYSICAL separation — no new substances formed.
commonMistakes: Confusing fractional distillation (physical) with cracking (chemical decomposition).
Saying lighter fractions have higher boiling points — it's the opposite.
clozePassages: Hydrocarbons are compounds containing only hydrogen and carbon atoms. They are the main components of crude oil, which is a mixture of hydrocarbons with different chain lengths. Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation — the mixture is heated and vapours rise up a fractionating column and condense at different levels depending on their boiling points. Shorter chains have lower boiling points and are more flammable.

Crude oil is a finite, non-renewable resource formed over millions of years from the remains of marine organisms. It is extracted by drilling and refined by fractional distillation. The fractions obtained include petrol, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, and bitumen. Each fraction is a mixture of hydrocarbons with similar chain lengths and boiling points. Crude oil is the raw material for many important products including fuels and plastics.

The physical properties of hydrocarbons depend on the length of their carbon chains. Shorter chains are more volatile (evaporate easily), have lower boiling points, and are less viscous. Longer chains have higher boiling points and are more viscous. These properties affect their uses — short-chain hydrocarbons are used as fuels (petrol, LPG) while long-chain hydrocarbons are used as lubricants and road surfacing (bitumen).

Alkanes.intro: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons — they contain only single C-C bonds. They are the main components of crude oil fractions.

sections.title: Alkane Structure
points: General formula: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
Only single C-C bonds — SATURATED
Methane CH₄, Ethane C₂H₆, Propane C₃H₈, Butane C₄H₁₀

sections.title: Combustion of Alkanes
points: Complete combustion (excess O₂): hydrocarbon + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O (blue flame)
Incomplete combustion (limited O₂): produces CO (toxic) and carbon (soot)
Carbon monoxide is toxic — binds to haemoglobin, preventing O₂ transport

keyTerms.def: Saturated hydrocarbon with general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
Contains only single C-C bonds — no double bonds
Burning in excess oxygen → CO₂ and H₂O
Burning in limited oxygen → CO and carbon (soot)

examTips: Complete combustion = CO₂ + H₂O (clean). Incomplete = CO + C (dirty, toxic).
Alkanes are saturated — do NOT decolourise bromine water.
commonMistakes: Saying incomplete combustion produces CO₂ — it produces CO (carbon monoxide).
clozePassages: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. They have only single carbon-carbon bonds. The first four alkanes are methane (CH₄), ethane (C₂H₆), propane (C₃H₈), and butane (C₄H₁₀). Alkanes are relatively unreactive because the C-C and C-H bonds are strong and non-polar. However, they undergo combustion reactions with oxygen and substitution reactions with halogens in UV light.

Complete combustion of alkanes occurs with excess oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water. Incomplete combustion occurs when oxygen is limited, producing carbon monoxide (a toxic gas) and soot (carbon particles). Complete combustion releases more energy than incomplete combustion. In car engines and gas boilers, ensuring complete combustion is important for both efficiency and safety.

Alkanes form a homologous series — a family of compounds with the same general formula and similar chemical properties, where each member differs by a CH₂ unit. As chain length increases, boiling point increases due to stronger intermolecular forces. All alkanes burn in oxygen. Their structural formulae show the arrangement of atoms — isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures, giving them different physical properties.

Alkenes.intro: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing a C=C double bond. They are more reactive than alkanes and used to make polymers.

sections.title: Alkene Structure
points: General formula: CₙH₂ₙ
Contain one C=C double bond — UNSATURATED
Ethene C₂H₄, Propene C₃H₆, Butene C₄H₈

callout.label: Bromine Water Test
callout.text: Add bromine water (orange). Alkene present → decolourises to colourless. Alkane → no change (stays orange).

sections.title: Addition Reactions
points: The C=C double bond opens up — atoms add across it
Hydrogenation: alkene + H₂ → alkane (nickel catalyst, 150°C)
Hydration: alkene + H₂O → alcohol (steam, phosphoric acid catalyst)
Halogenation: alkene + Br₂ → dibromoalkane (this decolourises bromine water)

keyTerms.def: Unsaturated hydrocarbon with C=C double bond; formula CₙH₂ₙ
Contains at least one C=C double bond
Atoms add across a C=C double bond — only one product formed

examTips: Bromine water test: alkenes decolourise it (orange → colourless); alkanes do not.
Addition reactions have 100% atom economy — all atoms end up in the product.
commonMistakes: Saying alkanes decolourise bromine water — only alkenes do this.
Forgetting that addition reactions produce only ONE product.
clozePassages: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with at least one carbon-carbon double bond. The general formula is CₙH₂ₙ. The simplest alkene is ethene (C₂H₄). The double bond makes alkenes more reactive than alkanes. They readily undergo addition reactions, where the double bond opens up and atoms are added across it. Alkenes decolourise bromine water — this is a test for unsaturation.

Alkenes undergo addition reactions. With hydrogen (hydrogenation), the double bond is broken and a single bond forms — ethene becomes ethane. With water (hydration), ethanol is produced — this is how ethanol is manufactured industrially. With halogens such as bromine, dihalogenoalkanes are produced. The bromine water test distinguishes alkenes from alkanes — alkenes decolourise bromine water while alkanes do not.

Addition polymerisation uses alkene monomers to form polymers. Ethene monomers join together under high pressure and temperature with a catalyst to form poly(ethene). Propene forms poly(propene). The double bonds in the monomers open up and form single bonds between monomers in the polymer chain. These polymers have many uses — packaging, fibres, and plastics. The repeat unit of the polymer has the same atoms as the monomer but with a single bond.

Cracking.intro: Cracking breaks large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones. It is essential because demand for shorter-chain fractions exceeds supply.

sections.title: Why Crack?
points: Crude oil contains too many long-chain fractions (not enough petrol, diesel)
Cracking converts surplus long chains into shorter, more useful ones
Also produces alkenes — essential for making polymers

sections.title: Types of Cracking
points: Thermal cracking: 700°C+, high pressure — mainly alkenes produced
Catalytic cracking: lower temperature (~500°C), aluminium oxide catalyst — mainly petrol and alkenes

callout.label: Example
callout.text: Decane (C₁₀H₂₂) → octane (C₈H₁₈) + ethene (C₂H₄). Always produces at least one alkene.

keyTerms.def: Breaking large hydrocarbons into smaller ones using heat (and sometimes a catalyst)
Cracking using aluminium oxide catalyst at ~500°C
Cracking using high temperature (700°C+) and pressure

examTips: Cracking always produces at least one alkene — important for polymer production.
Cracking is thermal decomposition — it needs heat and sometimes a catalyst.
commonMistakes: Saying cracking only produces alkanes — it always produces alkenes too.
Confusing cracking (chemical change) with fractional distillation (physical separation).
clozePassages: Cracking is the process of breaking long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful ones. It is carried out by heating the hydrocarbon to a high temperature and passing the vapour over a hot catalyst (catalytic cracking) or by heating to a very high temperature with steam (steam cracking). Cracking produces alkanes and alkenes, which are used as fuels and as raw materials for making polymers.

Crude oil contains more long-chain hydrocarbons than are needed and less short-chain hydrocarbons. Cracking converts the unwanted long-chain fractions into more useful shorter molecules. This includes petrol and other fuels, and alkenes such as ethene for making polymers. The cracking reaction produces a mixture of products. Alkenes are identified by their ability to decolourise bromine water.

There are two main types of cracking. Catalytic cracking uses a zeolite catalyst at moderate temperatures and produces branched alkanes and aromatic hydrocarbons, useful as petrol. Steam cracking uses high temperatures and steam and produces more alkenes, which are feedstocks for polymer production. Both types reduce the supply of long-chain fractions and increase the supply of more economically valuable shorter-chain products.

Polymers.intro: Polymers are very long chain molecules formed by joining many small monomer units together. Plastics are synthetic polymers.

sections.title: Addition Polymerisation
points: Unsaturated monomers (with C=C) join together
C=C double bond opens up, monomers join in a long chain
Only ONE product — 100% atom economy
Examples: ethene → poly(ethene); propene → poly(propene)

callout.label: Naming Rule
callout.text: Put 'poly' in front of the monomer name in brackets. E.g. ethene → poly(ethene). Propene → poly(propene).

sections.title: Issues with Plastics
points: Non-biodegradable — persist in environment for centuries
Microplastics enter food chains
Solutions: recycling, biodegradable plastics, reducing plastic use

keyTerms.def: A large molecule made of many repeating monomer units joined together
A small molecule that joins with others to form a polymer
Monomers with C=C bonds join together — no other products

examTips: Monomers need C=C bonds for addition polymerisation.
Name polymer by putting 'poly' before monomer name in brackets.
commonMistakes: Using alkanes as monomers — need alkenes (C=C double bonds).
Forgetting the brackets in polymer names — poly(ethene) not polyethene.
clozePassages: Addition polymers are formed from alkene monomers. The C=C double bond opens and monomers join in long chains. Poly(ethene) is used in plastic bags and bottles. Poly(propene) is used in ropes and containers. PVC (poly(chloroethene)) is used in pipes and window frames. The properties of the polymer depend on the monomer — chain length, branching, and cross-linking all affect strength and flexibility.

Condensation polymers form when monomers with two functional groups react, releasing a small molecule such as water. Polyester is made from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid. Nylon is a polyamide made from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid. Unlike addition polymers, condensation polymers have functional groups within the main chain. They can often be broken down by hydrolysis, which reverses the condensation reaction.

Disposing of polymers is a major environmental challenge. Most synthetic plastics are not biodegradable and persist in the environment for hundreds of years. Options include recycling, which requires sorting different polymer types. Some plastics can be broken down by combustion to recover energy. Biodegradable polymers made from plant starch are being developed as a more sustainable alternative. Reducing plastic use and improving recycling infrastructure are key priorities.

Alcohols and Carboxylic Acids.intro: Alcohols and carboxylic acids are important functional group families. Ethanol and ethanoic acid are the key examples.

sections.title: Alcohols
points: Functional group: -OH
General formula: CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH
Methanol CH₃OH, Ethanol C₂H₅OH, Propanol C₃H₇OH
Soluble in water; used as fuels and solvents
Ethanol made by: fermentation (glucose + yeast → ethanol + CO₂) or hydration of ethene

sections.title: Carboxylic Acids
points: Functional group: -COOH
Ethanoic acid CH₃COOH — found in vinegar
Weakly acidic — partially ionise in water
React with alcohols to form esters + water (esterification)
Esters have characteristic fruity smells — used in perfumes and flavourings

keyTerms.def: Organic compound containing an -OH functional group
Organic compound containing a -COOH functional group
Compound formed from alcohol + carboxylic acid — fruity smell
Anaerobic breakdown of glucose by yeast producing ethanol and CO₂

examTips: Esterification: alcohol + carboxylic acid → ester + water
Ethanoic acid is a WEAK acid — do not confuse with strong acids like HCl.
commonMistakes: Saying fermentation uses oxygen — it is an ANAEROBIC process.
clozePassages: Alcohols contain the hydroxyl functional group (-OH). The simplest alcohol is methanol (CH₃OH), followed by ethanol (C₂H₅OH) and propanol (C₃H₇OH). Ethanol is the alcohol found in alcoholic drinks, produced by fermentation of sugars. Alcohols are used as fuels, solvents, and in perfumes. They react with sodium to produce hydrogen gas and are oxidised to form carboxylic acids.

Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl functional group (-COOH). The simplest is methanoic acid, followed by ethanoic acid (found in vinegar). They are weak acids, partially ionising in water. Carboxylic acids react with alcohols in the presence of an acid catalyst to form esters and water — this is esterification. Esters have fruity smells and are used in perfumes and food flavourings.

Ethanol can be produced in two ways. Fermentation uses yeast to convert glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide — this is a slow process carried out at 30°C, suitable for making alcoholic drinks. Hydration of ethene with steam and an acid catalyst is a fast, continuous industrial process. Fermentation uses renewable plant material; hydration uses ethene from crude oil. Both methods have advantages depending on the context.
